'''Kwalhioqua–Clatskanie''' (Kwalhioqua–Tlatskanai, Lower Columbia Athabaskan) is an [[extinct language|extinct]] [[Athabaskan languages|Athabaskan language]] of northwest [[Oregon]] and southwest [[Washington (state)|Washington state]], along the lower [[Columbia River]]. It was documented in the early 20th century, and a wordlist was compiled, consisting of some 322 words.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Boas |first=Franz |last2=Goddard |first2=Pliny E. |date=July 1924 |title=Vocabulary of an Athapascan Dialect of the State of Washington |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/463748 |journal=International Journal of American Linguistics |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=39–45 |doi=10.1086/463748 |issn=0020-7071|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Dialects==
Dialects were:

* Kwalhioqua (a.k.a. Willapa or Willoopah) (north of the lower Columbia River)
**Willapa or Wela'pakote'li subdialect
**Suwal subdialect
* Clatskanie (a.k.a. Tlatskanai) (south of the lower Columbia River)

==Linguistic features==
Kwalhioqua-Clatskanie was likely most closely related to [[Tsilhqotʼin language|Tsilhqotʼin]] or [[Babine-Witsuwitʼen]], the latter of which is unique, along with Kwalhioqua-Clatskanie, in having a certain [[sound change]] from [[Proto-Athabaskan]].<ref name="krauss">{{Cite web |last=Krauss |first=Michael E. |year=1976b |title=Proto-Athabaskan–Eyak fricatives and the first person singular |url=https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/Online/CA961K1977a/krauss-1977-fricatives.pdf |id=CA961K1977a}}</ref>{{rp|48}} Other sound changes into Kwalhioqua-Clatskanie are unique in the family, and have helped Krauss reconstruct forms for the Proto-Athabaskan [[fricative]] series.<ref name="krauss" />{{rp|3}}

Kwalhioqua-Clatskanie had an optional [[distributive plural]] according to David Beck.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Beck |first=David |date=2000 |title=Grammatical Convergence and the Genesis of Diversity in the Northwest Coast Sprachbund |journal=Anthropological Linguistics |volume=42 |number=2 |page=159 |jstor=30028547}}</ref> It had a [[decimal number system]], a feature it shared with Athabaskan languages of southern Alaska, Oregon, and California.<ref name="dhymes">{{Cite journal |last=Dosch Hymes |first=Virginia |date=1955 |title=Athapaskan Numeral Systems |journal=International Journal of American Linguistics |volume=21 |number=1 |pages=26-45 |jstor=1263211}}</ref>{{rp|31}} Numerals for both dialects (Kwalhioqua and Clatskanie) were collected by Horatio Hale in 1840.<ref name="dhymes" />{{rp|41}}
